description: Somos o time responsável por transformar dados em soluções práticas e inteligência para o negócio. Nossa equipe conta com a coordenação de Vicente, liderando a estratégia da área, e com os Cientistas de Dados José Freitas e João Pedro, atuando lado a lado no desenvolvimento de modelos, análises e projetos de Inteligência Artificial.
summary:
QUADRA is a partner for smallholder farmers in Brazil's semi-arid Northeast, built to help with crop rotation: it improves what the farmer already plants today and recommends what would be ideal, based on the data. Online, the farmer picks a municipality, answers six questions and receives a three-year plan: the crop for each strip, when to plant, the expected income and a report.

Our focus is the scientific grounding of what really works: we distilled about 100 papers and technical manuals, including global meta-analyses (Mudare et al. 2025; Zhao et al. 2022), into 147 rotation configurations, each graded by evidence strength and transferability to the semi-arid. Numbers appear only when measured in a comparable climate.

The data: NASA (IMERG rainfall, POWER climate, SMAP soil moisture), Brazil's official climate-risk zoning and FAO GAEZ suitability, for 1,794 municipalities. The plan accounts for El Niño: each municipality shows how its rain behaved in the four strong El Niño years, as another is expected in 2026/27.

The system is efficient and pesticide-free: rotation, legumes and alternating strips break pest and disease cycles and feed the soil. Monoculture is never recommended. It matters because rainfed maize fails one year in five.
details:
What it does and how it works

QUADRA is a website that works as a partner for the smallholder farmer of Brazil's semi-arid Northeast. It starts from what the farmer plants today, improves it, and recommends what would be ideal for that land, based on the data.

On a 3D globe, the farmer finds the municipality (all 1,794 in the Northeast) and sees its rain, soil moisture and El Niño history.

Six questions with pictures: what you plant, plot size, type of soil, lowland, cassava cuttings and last year's crop.

The plan: a drawing of the plot in strips, with the crop of each strip for three years, comparing today's way with the ideal.

Earnings: the expected income of the plan against today's practice.

A printable report with planting and harvest dates.

Behind the screens, a Python engine chooses the crops that fit each municipality, using Brazil's official climate-risk zoning (ZARC) where it exists and FAO GAEZ v4 suitability elsewhere. It reads the climate from NASA POWER and GPM IMERG and the soil moisture from SMAP. The rotation rules come from a catalogue of 147 configurations, taken from about 100 papers and technical manuals.

Benefits

Advice the farmer can use: plain words, pictures, the plot measured in metres, on a phone, in English or Portuguese.

No pesticides and no monoculture: rotation, legumes and alternating strips break pest and disease cycles and feed the soil.

Honest numbers: they carry a label saying whether they were measured or assumed, and a number from a study appears only when it was measured in a comparable climate.

The farmer keeps the decision: the report is made to be discussed with the local extension agent.

Intended impact

Rainfed maize fails about one year in five in the Northeast, and a strong El Niño is expected in 2026/27. We want family farmers to enter each season with a plan that protects income and soil in dry years. The NASA and FAO data layers are global, so the method was designed to reach other dry regions; the local zoning is the piece that changes from country to country.

Tools, languages and data

Languages: Python (engine, server, data preparation and notebooks) and JavaScript, HTML and CSS (the site, with no framework).

Libraries: three.js (globe), MapLibre GL (map), pandas, NumPy, xarray, rasterio, GeoPandas and SciPy (data), and Jupyter (studies).

NASA data: POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP L4, and the Blue Marble and VIIRS Black Marble images (GIBS).

Other data: NOAA ONI (El Niño), FAO GAEZ v4, MAPA ZARC 2026/27, IBGE (yields, census and boundaries), CONAB (production costs) and OpenStreetMap.

Tests: Node.js and headless Microsoft Edge run an acceptance suite with more than 300,000 checks.

AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code, translate the site into English and summarize the papers, under the team's direction. Details are in the repository README.

Hardware: an ordinary personal computer. The site was designed for phone screens.

How it is creative

It grades science before using it: every rotation rule has a grade for strength of evidence (A to D) and another for how well it transfers to the semi-arid (T0 to T3).

It borrows percolation theory from physics to arrange the strips, so that plants of the same family do not form a continuous path for pests and diseases.

It starts from the farmer's reality, not from an ideal farm, and shows the two side by side.

It goes from orbit to the plot: the journey starts on the globe and ends in a drawing of the farmer's own field.

The name: "quadra" is what the people of the sertão call the rainy season.

Factors the team considered

The user: little time, a small screen and simple language.

Climate: El Niño, when the rain starts and how wet the soil is now.

Soil health: legumes, straw and deep roots, with no monoculture and no pesticides.

Money: income against today's practice, with official costs and yields.

Trust: where the evidence is weak, the site shows only the direction, not a number, and nothing is presented as a forecast.

Scale: global data first, local rules on top.
projectRefs: Kluger et al. 2025, Environmental Research Letters
